> Skyline is a custom flight controller for a quadcopter drone using the STM32F722 microcontroller. It will act as the brain of the drone, using an IMU sensor to detect movement and orientation and a barometer to estimate altitude. The board receive commands from a radio receiver and send signals to four ESCs to control the motors and help keep the drone stable. It also have USB-C for connectivity, a microSD card for flight data logging, and battery voltage monitoring. I'm designing the schematic and PCB in KiCad, adapting Hack Club's rocket flight controller guide for a drone.

### 2026-11-08: Nov 5-7: Skyline drone flight controller. Schematic

**15h**

Nov 5-7: Skyline drone flight controller. Schematic

I spent hours on this and honestly I'm tired. Skyline is a drone flight controller based on the Hack Club guide (https://blueprint.hackclub.com/starter-projects/flightcontroller), which is made for a rocket. So half the work was figuring out what a drone needs that a rocket doesn't.
 Turning a rocket into a drone
* 2 servo outputs became 4 motor outputs going to an 8-pin ESC header
* Added a receiver header (UART), a programming header (SWD) and battery voltage sensing
* The guide's BQ25883 charger only works with a 2S battery, and the 5V regulator maxes out at 16V. I wanted a bigger drone (4S is 16.8V), so both had to go
* I'm hand soldering and the IMU and barometer have pads hidden under the chip. So I replaced them with pin headers for breakout boards
* Power now comes through two diodes (USB or battery, whichever is higher) into the 3.3V regulator. USB-only power will be a bit marginal (~4.6V), so I need to test that on the real board

Firstly i went to the LCSC platform i searched all the components then I ran python lcsc.py lcsc.txt in the “black window” (the Command Prompt) from my hardware folder. The script uses a tool called easyeda2kicad to download each part’s symbol, footprint and 3D model into a lib folder, which I then added to KiCad as a library.

The power problem (the part I spent the longest on)
This is where the rocket design and a drone really disagree.
The BQ25883 is a charger for a 2-cell (2S) battery only.
The TPS63070 5V regulator can take at most about 16 V in.
A 4S battery is 16.8 V when full, and a 3S is 12.6 V.

I started by planning around 2S, but then decided I wanted a bigger drone, which usually means 4S. That broke two parts of the guide's power design at the same time. I also realised that charging on a drone board with no balancing isn't a good idea, so I'd charge with a proper hobby balance charger instead.

My hand-soldering decision made it worse. The BMP580, ICM-45686, BQ25883 and TPS63070 all have pads underneath the chip, so a normal soldering iron can't reach them so I removed the charger and the 5V regulator (and the battery screw terminal). The battery plugs into the 4-in-1 ESC, and the ESC's 8-pin plug brings battery power to my board.
Two SS34 Schottky diodes feed the main power rail VSYS: one from USB (VBUS) and one from the battery (BAT+)
The LMR51430 runs from VSYS. It accepts up to 36 V, so it's fine on 4S.
Re-did the battery divider for 4S.
Capacitors on the battery side need to be rated 25 V or more.
Added I2C pull-ups, since the charger used to provide them.
Replaced the IMU and barometer chips with pin headers (a 7-pin header for the IMU, and a 5-pin header for the barometer) so I can plug in ready-made breakout boards. I did this to keep the board hand-solderable.

I was nervous about deleting parts because I was almost done but did it anyway..(thats life yk hehe)

### 2026-11-08: Nov 7-9

**8h**

Nov 7-9
PCB layout and routing
I imported everything into the PCB editor, grouped parts (STM32, USB-C, power, microSD, connectors) and placed them so related parts sit close, with decoupling caps right at their STM32 pins. At first it was just a pile of overlapping parts and blue ratlines everywhere. I hid the ratlines while placing and planned to handle ground with a pour.

![Screenshot 2026-11-07 215958](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/gfWl2tMDbbFllUPCOWxRpQb4XDb3SDLx/6bf55de6a23c58edadd89410df94491f29deb074b8ddf53d759f1b93cf1db23e.png)
![Screenshot 2026-11-07 220422](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/gfWl2tMDbbFllUPCOWxRpQb4XDb3SDLx/a6597f2bb4d79436dd9dcd64309acd5fa0043744e04a774a017a739b023625f3.png)
Routing took way longer than I expected.
Tracks blocked each other constantly. I'd be unable to reach a pad because another track was in the way, so I moved parts, rerouted, edited schematic and used vias to switch between front and back copper.
USB-C confused me. I accidentally used differential pair routing and kept getting "Can't find a suitable starting point".
Some STM32 pin assignments made routing awful. I went back to the schematic and changed net labels, then had to figure out how to update the PCB without losing the routing I'd already done.
I mixed up saved versions of the project and thought I lost all my work a KiCad window saved over my organised layout, so I had to restore.
